supplementary_info.identification_information: Tiliqua rugosa rugosa is variable in colour, generally brown, olive brown, to black with irregular pale bands on the body and tail, the head is often boldly flushed with orange red. T. r. konowi is smaller with less variable colour, usually a dark grey with pale peppering above and below. T. r. aspera is more robust and varies in colour without the red flushing on the head. T. r. palarra has a relatively narrow, dark, head with pale streaks and spots, and a large brown mid ventral patch (Wilson and Swan 2013).

documentation.range: This species is endemic to Australia, where it is found from the south west of Western Australia, across the Great Australia Bight to the west of New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland. Tiliqua rugosa rugosa occurs in the southwest and T. r. konowi is only found on Rottnest Island. T. r. aspera occurs across the Nullabor Plain into eastern Queensland, and T. r. palarra is found on the mid-west coast from Shark Bay to Carnarvon in Western Australia (Wilson and Swan 2013). It has an eastern and southern range limit at the Great Dividing Range; records from west of this Range either represent misidentifications or human transport, probably linked to the pet trade (C. Sanderson pers. comm. 2017)
documentation.population: This species is common. Tiliqua rugosa konowi may be experiencing population declines, or may have historically as a result of cat predation on Rottnest Island, and as a result of ongoing illegal targeted collection.
documentation.habitats: Tiliqua rugosa inhabits dry to arid open habitats, including mallee woodlands, shrublands and coastal dunes (Wilson and Swan 2013), and also eucalypt forests. This species shelters under dome shaped bushes with low foliage, and thorny bushes (Kerr et al. 2003). It can be found in degraded areas, including agricultural land and peri-urban landscapes. This species is monogamous and mates for life.
documentation.threats: No significant threats have been identified for Tiliqua rugosa. Collection is a local pressure on the Rottnest populations, but it is not clear that this is presently a major threat.
documentation.measures: In Western Australia, Tiliqua rugosa konowi is listed as Vulnerable (Macdonald 2012, DPaW 2015). There are no specific conservation actions in place for this species. However the range coincides with protected areas, such as the Rottnest Island Nature Reserve, and this species may benefit from management plans of areas of their habitat, such as the Herdsman Lake Regional Park Management Plan (CALM 2004, Wilson and Swan 2013).
documentation.use_trade: With the appropriate licences, this species can be kept in captivity as a pet (DPaW 2016). It is found in the international pet trade. There is particular commercial interest in the Rottnest subspecies, which is excluded from legal collection, and illegal harvesting from Rottnest is an ongoing threat.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern on the basis that this species is common, adaptable and extremely widespread, and there are no major threats to most subspecies.
